https://www.dumbartonreporter.co.uk/news.text: Ryanair warns of long EES queues at 16 European airports Entry Exit System Ryanair Leisure Travel By Patrick Glover Trending News Reporter Share 0 Comments The EU's Entry/Exit System (EES) continues to cause disruptions. (Image: Getty Images) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Ryanair has warned Brits travelling to Europe this summer to expect "significant" queues at 16 major airports. The warning comes as the European Union 's Entry/Exit System (EES) continues to create disruptions, months after its introduction. The EES was first introduced in October last year, before the rollout ramped up on April 10. The new system requires British travellers and other non-EU visitors to provide biometric data, including fingerprints and facial scans, when entering the Schengen Area. The new EES has received significant backlash since its introduction, with it causing long waits for passengers at airports. Some travellers have already experienced waits of up to six hours, and industry experts warn these disruptions could continue for up to two years . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Portugal Travel Advisor | Julia T (@travel_luckk) Major airlines, including Jet2 and Ryanair, have called for the rollout of the new system to be suspended until after the summer to allow for a "smoother airport experience" during peak travel season. CEO of Malta Air, David O’Brien, even threatened to pull all flights to Malta due to the extended wait times caused by the EES at airports. EES to cause long queues at these 16 major airports this summer Brits heading to Europe this summer have been told to expect more delays due to the EES. Ryanair has outlined 16 European Airports where travellers can expect "significant" queues: Tenerife South Palma/Majorca Alicante Malaga Milan Bergamo Krakow Paris Beauvais Lisbon Madrid Lanzarote Milan Malpensa Verona Berlin Cologne Frankfurt Hahn Budapest Chief operations officer at Ryanair, Neal McMahon, said: "Families heading away for a well-earned summer holiday should be thinking about suitcases, suncream and sangria, not standing in passport queues for hours. "The reality is that the EES system isn’t working properly and families are paying the price for a system that does not work months after launch. "Passengers should not be the testing ground for unfished border infrastructure." Mr McMahon has backed calls from EU Member States to extend current EES flexibilities into early 2027. This extension would give airports and border authorities more time to fix malfunctioning kiosks, increase staffing levels, and ensure the system can operate efficiently before full enforcement is introduced. He said: "We support calls from EU Member States to urgently extend the EES flexibilities. "This will give airports and border authorities the time to improve the infrastructure, fix the broken devices and hire more staff so that families can travel through Europe without disruption." Ryanair has advised UK passengers travelling to and from non-Schengen destinations, or transiting through affected European airports, to allow extra time for their journey and be prepared for lengthy waits at passport control. ETIAS launch delayed until 2027 Meanwhile, the launch of the EU's new European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) has been delayed until 2027 . The ETIAS is a pre-authorisation scheme which will apply to UK passport holders and other visa-exempt travellers entering 30 European countries for short stays. Applicants will be required to pay a €20 fee, though travellers under 18 or over 70 will be exempt. The ETIAS was expected to launch later this year, but it has now been delayed until 2027, according to the Financial Times . The decision is due to "technical glitches" and delays with the EES, which only recently came online after being postponed from 2022. EU home affairs commissioner, Magnus Brunner, said the delays were due to "other factors", including insufficient staff or lack of adequate infrastructure. EU-Lisa, the agency responsible for ETIAS, has reportedly acknowledged that "launching it by the end of this year as planned was no longer feasible". The European Commission will set the official launch date only after EU-Lisa confirms the system has been fully tested and is ready. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-civil-so.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5LVsP In 2024, hundreds of thousands across the country rallied in protest against right-wing extremism Image: Stefan Boness/IPON/picture alliance Advertisement Fighting for democracy and human rights in Germany today means mustering up a lot of courage. For Felix Pankonin , locking and checking all doors and windows around the house has become practically second nature. Sometimes, a hot-tempered lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party shows up on his property. Pankonin's bicycles have been vandalized, and he has received threats that something will happen to his animals. Most recently, his partner was physically assaulted. Pankonin is the project director of educational programs on political issues, Jewish history and antisemitism at the Hillersche Villa in Zittau, in the eastern German state of Saxony . The situation is similar for Keerthana Kuperan, who works as a political adviser at DaMOst , the umbrella organization for migrant groups in eastern Germany. Kuperan, whose parents are from Sri Lanka, said right-wing extremism has had a major impact on her work over the past three years. "We have completely different security protocols now. After 6 p.m. no one is left alone in the office, and when putting up posters in rural areas, security measures are put in place beforehand," she said. Kuperan's work is primarily focused on ensuring the safety of activists. Another aspect of her work involves dealing with challenges from the AfD, which files parliamentary information requests, often on migration, in order to delay political proceedings and highlight issues that should not really be controversial. Ahead of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, numerous business owners with a background of migration went on strike against racism and fascism, and in support of a free and democratic society Image: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance In Saxony-Anhalt , a federal state with a very low proportion of foreigners, state legislative elections will be held on September 6. DaMOst observes that the political landscape has shifted to the right. This has led to the discrediting of democratic networks, which has affected their funding and job opportunities. Green Party politician becomes target of hostilities Miriam Zeller, a city councilor in Stendal, a city of 37,000 in northern Saxony-Anhalt, is a member of the environmentalist Green Party and is running in the election. Zeller told DW that the hostility against her was even more intense when the Greens were in power. Her daughter stopped being invited to birthday parties, and she herself was viciously accused of being a warmonger. From the very beginning, the Greens had declared their solidarity with Ukraine after it had come under attack from Russia. "It can't get any worse than this," said Zeller. Miriam Zeller, a Green Party candidate, has also felt the impact of the shift to the right in her private life Image: Miriam Zeller However, she pointed out that, fortunately, as a teacher, she is a civil servant and therefore cannot lose her job. For others, the specter of losing one's job — should the AfD come to power — is very real. Alliance for Democracy: Educating people on how to defend themselves The Together for Democracy alliance aims to support individuals or institutions that are being attacked or threatened by far-right extremists — people like Pankonin, Kuperan and Zeller. The aim of the group's Solidarity Agreement — which over 80 groups have signed, including labor unions, the major Christian churches, sports organizations, human rights groups as well as social and environmental organizations — is to ensure that anyone who is targeted for their commitment to democracy will not be left alone. The groups joined forces in 2024 to form an alliance against the far right when it became clear that attacks on democracy were intensifying. Now, alliance members want to also offer help and support in the event of attacks on youth or cultural centers, hate campaigns against people who speak out publicly, or when volunteers are threatened — whether through public expressions of solidarity or by providing legal or financial support. The alliance includes powerful actors such as the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) and environmental organizations like Greenpeace. Yasmin Fahimi, the head of the DGB, which has over 5 million members, took the opportunity to present the new agreement in Berlin. When asked by DW whether the AfD, in the event of an election victory, could actually fire all public employees, Fahimi was clear. "This fantasy of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt — to carry out a complete personnel shake-up in government agencies, ministries, courts and the police — is completely unlawful," Fahimi said. "We are making it clear to our members that they can fight back against this. It is also a manifestation of an authoritarian mindset to believe that one can simply issue a decree and do as one pleases. That's not how our democracy works." That is why the DGB is training its members both in constitutional law and civil service law so they can defend themselves, Fahimi said. The trade union leader has called for more commitment from politicians. "We must ensure — especially in regional areas, but also within our institutions — that people cannot simply be forced to comply with unlawful orders. I believe it would be good for the Conference of Interior Ministers to discuss how to provide clear information, seminars and workshops on these issues, so that public servants, ministry employees and staff at institutions governed by the rule of law are not left to fend for themselves," she said. Threats, abuse to German mayors hurting local government To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Teaming up to hlep 'bring this injustice to light' "Of course, this alliance can mean more protection for queer people who are active on the ground," said Andre Lehmann, from the Queer Diversity Association (LSVD+) — a civil rights organization that has represented the interests and concerns of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans* and intersex queer people ( LGBTQ+ ) since 1990. "Right now, we're seeing a lot of attacks on Pride events all over Germany. In some cases, local organizers don't even know what to do in such situations. That's where an alliance like this can step in," Lehmann told DW. The Islamist attack on the Pride event in Berlin has deeply unsettled the queer community, said Lehmann. On top of that, many democracy projects are being financially bled dry right now. The alliance will hardly be able to make up for the lack of funding for democracy projects that has resulted from the federal government's cuts and restructuring. However, teaming up with other organizations helps build strength, said Sophie Lampl, who works for Greenpeace. "That is certainly one of the strengths we can bring as an environmental organization: our ability to campaign. To provide support when civil society organizations or individuals are attacked, to publicly stand up for them and to bring this injustice to light," Lampl said. Will the alliance also be able to help in rural areas? Pankonin has often helped the Together for Democracy alliance — by providing legal advice, funding for security and moral support. Pankonin would like to see more involvement from major organizations in rural areas. Green Party politician Zeller reports that she has also received aid from small local networks. She believes that a large network, with its newfound solidarity, can make a big difference and could be a vital source of support, even in rural areas. For his part, Lehmann is determined. "We will defend our democracy and, if necessary, guide our local people through this valley," he said. This article was originally written in German. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/a-t.text: The Budapest Times A tale of two Hungarys: PM vows to bridge the urban-rural divide The government is launching the Saint Stephen rural development programme, the Prime Minister said at Tuesday's session of the National Assembly, before the agenda. Péter Magyar announced that they are already working on a proposal aimed at abolishing the "hollowed-out" county assemblies and completely overhauling the system. The Prime Minister stressed that just over a year ago, still as an opposition party, on 20 August — Saint Stephen’s Day — they had made a promise to the Hungarian countryside and its villages, to those people who “have been living, working, raising families, farming, running businesses and building communities in their homeland for generations.” He recalled that they had pledged to provide a community development fund of one billion forints per year for every ten settlements. He added that they had also committed to not dictating from Budapest how that money should be spent. Péter Magyar emphasised that they tell ten settlements to sit down together and decide for themselves what they need, “and we will provide the funding.” This will form the basis of the Saint Stephen programme, the Prime Minister said. He explained that Hungarian politics has long had an outstanding debt to the Hungarian countryside, as in recent decades “people living in villages have been looked down on far too often,” exploited too often, and deceived too often. “There were times when their votes were needed, times when their loyalty was needed, and times when all that was expected of them was to stay silent,” he said. He said: if a country fails for decades to offer a vision to young people in rural areas, there are consequences. Young people move away, schools close, shops close, there is less work, it becomes increasingly harder to run a business, doctors become ever more distant, and then at some point the question for a settlement is no longer how it can develop, but how it can survive, he explained. Péter Magyar stated that over recent decades, rural communities had received from politics not genuine help, partnership, or respect, but division — “a hypocritical politics that turned Hungarians against one another.” Those living in villages were deliberately placed on one side, on one bank of an artificially dug trench, and were told that what happens in the cities is suspicious, what comes from Budapest is bad, and what happens abroad is dangerous, he said. He continued: rural people were told that anyone who thinks differently is an enemy, anyone who lives differently poses a threat, and anyone who votes for another party is less Hungarian. Meanwhile, on the other side, “the former left-wing satellite parties of Fidesz” were insinuating to city dwellers that people living in villages are backward, do not understand the world, and cannot be reasoned with. The prime ministerial candidate stated: enough is enough of politicians spending decades making a living by turning Hungarians against one another. Enough of trench-digging and fear-mongering, enough of telling one half of the country “to fear the other,” he said. Péter Magyar emphasized that Budapest is not the enemy of rural Hungary, the village is not the enemy of the city, the farmer is not the enemy of the city dweller, the rural person is no less modern, and the city person is no less Hungarian. He stated that a strong Hungary cannot exist without strong local communities, and that rural Hungary and Budapest are not enemies — “we are one country.” He recalled that they had committed to providing a community development fund of one billion forints per ten settlements annually, alongside the Magyar Falu Program and the Versenyképes Járások Program. He announced that they are now launching the implementation of this commitment: the Szent István rural development programme. According to his account, the new system will first be piloted in ten rural micro-regions — in the areas around Zalakaros, Harkány, Bács, Pásztó, Medgyesegyháza, Igal, Tiszaújváros, Gyöngyös, Nyírbátor, and Gönc — across a total of one hundred settlements, involving nearly one hundred thousand people. He said that in these ten regions, average per capita income falls 36.7 percent below the national average. Péter Magyar said that in the coming months, people living locally and experts will jointly assess the opportunities and problems of each region, together draw up the development strategy, and jointly compile those investment plans that are genuinely feasible both professionally and financially — after which local residents will say what matters to them. The prime minister said that previous governments had deliberately hollowed out county assemblies and turned them into squalid payoff centres, which today function solely as “payoff centres for the failed parties of the fragmented opposition.” He accused the opposition parties of using county assemblies as “public money ATMs.” He added that the assemblies had been turned into a place where “the remaining tentacles of the original Fidesz, the green Fidesz, and the blue Fidesz can collude together over EU tenders.” One or two days a month, and multimillion-forint salaries fly out the door, while the county gains nothing from the work of the assemblies, the prime minister assessed. He noted that he was not referring to the few remaining professionals still working in county assemblies, but to “the Fidesz and other opposition feudal lords” who use the county assemblies to intimidate village mayors and who rule over their remaining domains “as county landlords.” Péter Magyar said that this was also why they had halted the “unchecked spending of public funds” by abolishing the expense allowances of county assembly presidents and vice-presidents and reducing the multimillion-forint salaries of assembly leaders. Péter Magyar stressed that it was time to move forward and that this system must be brought to an end; they are already working on a proposal aimed at abolishing the hollowed-out county assemblies and completely overhauling the system. The prime minister stated that the country would be able to save, and will save, tens of billions of forints annually from the tax money of rural residents, funds that could be directed toward development programmes. The money of the Hungarian people will finally end up in the right place, once the “public money dispensers at the county assemblies” used by opposition parties are dismantled, he stressed, adding that it is worth considering what does and does not belong in the county self-government system. The prime minister described the most pressing question of rural policy as what must be done to keep young people from leaving. We cannot tell a twenty-year-old to stay home, start a family, and build a business locally, while there are no jobs, no nurseries nearby, the roads are poor, and there is no adequate internet or other infrastructure, he pointed out. He emphasised that patriotism and a sense of belonging are important, but people must also be able to make a living, and for that reason the government is building a countryside where leaving or staying is a matter of free choice rather than necessity. Péter Magyar described one of the greatest mistakes of recent decades as the gradual weaning of local communities off making decisions about their own futures. “Someone always came from above” — “most often the local lord of the manor at the village fair” — to dictate what was best. The Tisza government takes the knowledge and needs of local residents seriously, he promised by contrast. He stated that the initial phase of the Szent István Programme, covering 10 regions, will be evaluated, and that a national rural and regional development network will be built on that basis. After 20 August 2027, the nationwide rollout of the programme may begin. According to current plans, the Szent István rural development programme could directly benefit 2,174 rural settlements and approximately 1 million 850 thousand Hungarian people, he said.
